title: Grade 4 SOCIAL STUDIES — 4.3 Enterprise Project at School

pages.lesson:
PAGE 1: Overview

OVERVIEW
========

An enterprise is a small project people start in order to produce something useful and, often, to earn some income. In this sub-strand you will identify projects a school can start, help to plan and run one, share the work fairly, and keep honest records.

## Strand 4.0: Resources and Economic Activities
Sub-strand 4.3: Enterprise Project at School
Suggested lessons: 7

## Learning outcomes
By the end of the sub-strand, the learner should be able to:
a) identify the projects that can be initiated at school
b) participate in initiating an enterprise project at school
c) uphold ethics and collective efforts in managing enterprise projects at school

## Key inquiry questions
1. How are enterprise projects managed in school?

## Core competencies
• Communication and collaboration: Learners share responsibilities on the planned enterprise
• Creativity and imagination: Learners identify a viable project enterprise at school

## Values
• Responsibility: Learners engage in the assigned roles and duties as they undertake the enterprise project at school and evaluate its success
• Integrity: Learners develop accountability as they participate in the initiation and management of the enterprise project in the school

## Pertinent and contemporary issues
• Creative and critical thinking: Learners undertake the enterprise project at school and showcase the outcomes.

## Links to other learning areas
• Mathematics: Learners plan and undertake a viable enterprise project at school.

## Source
• KICD Grade 4 Social Studies Curriculum Design (Revised 2024) — Strand 4.0 Resources and Economic Activities, Sub-strand 4.3 Enterprise Project at School

PAGE 2: Lesson 1: Projects a school can start

LESSON 1: PROJECTS A SCHOOL CAN START
=====================================

## What you will learn
• Explain what an enterprise project is.
• Identify projects that can be started at school.

Curriculum outcomes: a) identify the projects that can be initiated at school

## Introduction
Some schools grow vegetables behind the classrooms and sell the extra to teachers and parents. The garden is not only a farm. It is a small business that learners help to run.

## Notes
An enterprise is a project started to produce goods or services. A school enterprise is run by learners and teachers together, on the school grounds or with the school's permission. The aim is to learn how work is planned, to produce something useful, and sometimes to raise a little money for the project or the school.

### Projects that suit a primary school
A project should be possible for learners of your age, with adults nearby:

- A vegetable garden, selling surplus sukuma wiki, tomatoes or onions
- A tree nursery, raising seedlings to plant or sell
- Poultry, such as a few chickens, if the school has a safe house for them and an adult in charge
- Crafts, such as woven mats, decorated cards or simple beadwork using local materials
- A recycling project that collects clean bottles or paper for sale to a buyer
- Making simple road-safety items, such as bright sashes, to use in a school safety campaign or to sell at a school event

Not every idea is suitable. A project that needs dangerous machines, takes learners out of class for whole days, or breaks the law is not a school enterprise.

### How to spot a possible project
Look at what the school already has: land, water, learners who can work, and people who might buy the product. Also look at a need. If the road near school is busy, a safety campaign may be useful. If the kitchen buys vegetables every week, a garden may have a ready market.

## Key words
• enterprise — a project started to produce goods or services, often to earn some income
• project — a planned piece of work with a goal
• surplus — what is left after the producers have taken what they need

## Worked examples

### Example 1
Learners want to open a stone quarry and miss lessons to break rocks. Is this a suitable school enterprise?

Working:
1. The work is dangerous.
2. It takes children out of school.
3. Forcing children to do such work is child labour.

Answer: No. It is dangerous, it replaces learning, and it is not lawful child work.

### Example 2
The school kitchen buys vegetables every week, and there is an empty plot with water nearby. Suggest one enterprise.

Working:
1. There is land, water and a buyer.

Answer: A vegetable garden.

## Activity: Brainstorm school enterprises
You will need: Manila paper, Marker pens
1. In groups, brainstorm enterprise projects that can be undertaken at your school.
2. For each idea, write what you would produce and who might use or buy it.
3. Cross out any idea that is dangerous or would stop you attending lessons.
4. Present three possible projects to the class.

## Practice
1. What is a school enterprise project?
2. Name three projects a school could start.
3. Why is a quarry project not suitable for Grade 4 learners?

## Summary
• A school enterprise produces something useful and teaches learners how work is organised.
• Gardens, nurseries, crafts and recycling can fit a primary school.
• Dangerous work that replaces lessons is not a school project.

### Answers to practice
1. A project run by learners and teachers to produce goods or services and to learn how a small business is managed.
2. Any three: a vegetable garden, a tree nursery, poultry, crafts, recycling, or making simple road-safety items.
3. It is dangerous and it would take children away from school.

PAGE 3: Lesson 2: Choosing a viable project

LESSON 2: CHOOSING A VIABLE PROJECT
===================================

## What you will learn
• Explain what makes a project viable.
• Choose one viable enterprise for the class or school.

Curriculum outcomes: a) identify the projects that can be initiated at school; b) participate in initiating an enterprise project at school

## Introduction
A good idea can still fail if there is no water, no buyer or no one to do the work. Viable means the project can actually succeed with what you have.

## Notes
A viable project is one that can work. Before the class begins, test the idea with simple questions.

### Questions that test an idea
- Need: do people want this product or service?
- Resources: do we have land, water, materials or a safe space?
- Skills: can learners do the work with a teacher helping?
- Time: can the work be done at agreed times without missing lessons?
- Cost: can the school or parents provide the first materials, or can we start very small?
- Market: who will use or buy the product?
- Rules: has the head teacher agreed? Does the project obey the law and school rules?
- Care: will the project harm the soil, waste water or leave animals without shelter? If yes, change the plan.

### Comparing ideas
Write two or three ideas in a table. Give each question a yes or a no. The idea with more yes answers is the stronger one. If a garden has land and a buyer but a poultry house would cost more than the school can raise, the garden is more viable this term.

Creativity is useful here. A class with no spare land might grow vegetables in sacks, or make cards from used paper. A small start is wiser than a huge plan that stops in the first week.

The class should agree together. Forcing one group’s idea on everyone, without listening, makes the project hard to manage later.

## Key words
• viable — able to succeed with the resources and time available
• market — the people who will use or buy what you produce
• cost — the money or materials needed to start and run a project

## Worked examples

### Example 1
Idea A needs a borehole the school does not have. Idea B uses rainwater already stored in a tank. Which is more viable this term, and why?

Working:
1. Idea A depends on something the school cannot provide now.
2. Idea B uses water the school already has.

Answer: Idea B, because the water it needs is already available.

### Example 2
A class wants to keep ten cows. They have a small flower bed and no grazing. What should they decide?

Working:
1. Cows need space and feed the school does not have.

Answer: The project is not viable. They should choose a smaller project, such as vegetables in sacks or a tree nursery.

## Activity: Choose one viable enterprise
You will need: Manila paper, The list of ideas from the previous lesson
1. Draw a table with your best three ideas.
2. Answer yes or no for need, resources, skills, time, cost, market and the head teacher's permission.
3. Choose the idea with the most yes answers.
4. Tell the class why it is viable and what you will produce.

## Practice
1. What does viable mean?
2. Name four things to check before starting a school enterprise.
3. Why might sack gardens be a better start than a large farm?

## Summary
• A viable project fits the school's space, money, time and skills.
• Compare ideas before choosing.
• Start small enough to finish.

### Answers to practice
1. Able to succeed with the time, skills and resources the school actually has.
2. Any four: need, resources, skills, time, cost, buyers, permission and care for the environment.
3. They need little space and little money, so the class can manage them.

PAGE 4: Lesson 3: Planning the enterprise

LESSON 3: PLANNING THE ENTERPRISE
=================================

## What you will learn
• List the materials, costs and steps of a school enterprise.
• Use simple addition to find the cost of the plan.

Curriculum outcomes: b) participate in initiating an enterprise project at school

## Introduction
A garden does not appear because the class likes vegetables. Someone must list the seeds, the tools, the watering days and what to do if the rain fails.

## Notes
A plan is a list of steps written before the work begins. It stops the class from forgetting tools, overspending or arguing about who should do what.

### What the plan contains
- The goal: what we will produce, and by when
- Materials: seeds, tins, soil, water, paper, cloth or feed
- Where the materials will come from: school store, home, or a small purchase
- Cost: the price of anything that must be bought
- A calendar: which days the class will work, and for how long
- Roles: who leads, who records, who handles any money, who does each task
- Permission: the head teacher's signature or spoken agreement
- A rule for profit: if anything is sold, where the money will go

### Counting the cost
Add the prices of the items you must buy. If seeds cost 50 shillings and a watering can costs 200 shillings, the start-up cost is 250 shillings. Items brought from home have a cost of zero shillings in the school record, but you still list them so that nobody forgets.

If the total is more than the class can raise, reduce the plan. Ten packets of seed may be too many. Two packets may be enough for a first bed.

Write the plan neatly. Mathematics helps here: adding costs, counting seedlings and sharing tasks in equal turns. A plan that lives only in somebody's head is easily forgotten or changed unfairly.

## Key words
• plan — steps written down before work begins
• start-up cost — the money needed to begin a project
• goal — what the project is trying to achieve

## Worked examples

### Example 1
Seeds cost 40 shillings, string costs 20 shillings and a notebook for records costs 30 shillings. What is the start-up cost?

Working:
1. Add the three prices.
2. 40 + 20 = 60, and 60 + 30 = 90.

Answer: 90 shillings.

### Example 2
The class needs 500 shillings but can only raise 200. What should they do?

Working:
1. The plan costs more than they have.
2. A smaller plan may still be viable.

Answer: Reduce the plan so that the cost is not more than 200 shillings.

## Activity: Write the project plan
You will need: Exercise book, Prices from a local shop or from the teacher, Manila paper
1. Write the goal of the viable project you chose.
2. List materials. Mark which ones you already have and which must be bought.
3. Add the costs of the items to be bought.
4. Write the steps from the first day to the day you will showcase the product.
5. Show the plan to the teacher and correct anything that is missing.

## Practice
1. Name four things a project plan should contain.
2. Tins cost 15 shillings and seeds cost 25 shillings. What is the total?
3. Why should the plan be written down?

## Summary
• A plan lists the goal, materials, cost, time and roles.
• Add costs before you begin, and shrink the plan if it is too expensive.
• The head teacher should agree to the plan.

### Answers to practice
1. Any four: the goal, materials, costs, calendar, roles, permission and a rule for any money earned.
2. 40 shillings.
3. So that steps, costs and duties are not forgotten or changed unfairly.

PAGE 5: Lesson 4: Sharing the work

LESSON 4: SHARING THE WORK
==========================

## What you will learn
• Share responsibilities for the enterprise.
• Explain why collective effort helps a project succeed.

Curriculum outcomes: b) participate in initiating an enterprise project at school; c) uphold ethics and collective efforts in managing enterprise projects at school

## Introduction
If only one learner waters the garden, the work stops whenever that learner is absent. When the class shares the duties, the project can continue.

## Notes
Collective effort means working together towards one goal. Each person does a part, and the parts add up to the finished project.

### Useful roles
Schools may use these roles. The names can change, but the duties should be clear:

- Chairperson: calls the group to order and makes sure everyone is heard
- Secretary: writes decisions, dates and work done
- Treasurer: keeps the money record with the teacher. Learners do not take project money home.
- Team leaders: each watches one task, such as watering, weeding, collecting materials or preparing the showcase

Roles should rotate so that many learners learn each skill. A role is a duty, not a chance to boss others or to escape work.

### Starting the work
On the first day, gather the materials in the plan, mark the plot or the workspace, and do the first task together. The teacher stays with the class. At the end, the secretary records what was done and what is needed next time.

### When someone is away
Agree a substitute before you need one. If the watering team is at a match, another team waters. Collective effort fails when people say 'that is not my work' while the plants dry up.

Listen to quiet learners as well as to loud ones. A good idea about pests or about a cheaper material can come from anybody.

## Key words
• collective effort — people working together, each doing a share of the task
• role — the duty a person is given in a group
• treasurer — the person who keeps the record of money, together with the teacher

## Worked examples

### Example 1
The treasurer wants to keep the project money in a pocket over the weekend. What should happen instead?

Working:
1. Project money can be lost or misused.
2. The teacher is responsible with the learners.

Answer: The money should stay in the school office or with the teacher, and the record should be written the same day.

### Example 2
Only the chairperson has been allowed to speak for three weeks. What is wrong?

Working:
1. Collective effort needs many voices.
2. Roles should not silence the group.

Answer: Other learners are not being heard. The chairperson should invite them to speak, and roles should be shared.

## Activity: Share responsibilities
You will need: The project plan, Exercise book
1. List the tasks in the plan.
2. Agree roles: chairperson, secretary, treasurer with the teacher, and task teams.
3. Write each person's duty for the next two weeks.
4. Decide who covers a task if someone is absent.
5. Start the first task together and let the secretary record it.

## Practice
1. What is collective effort?
2. What does the secretary do?
3. Why should project money stay at school?

## Summary
• Shared roles keep the project going when one person is away.
• The treasurer works with the teacher and does not take money home.
• Everyone should be heard.

### Answers to practice
1. Working together so that each person does a share of the project.
2. Writes down decisions, dates and the work that has been done.
3. So that it is not lost or used for a private purpose, and so that the record stays with the project.

PAGE 6: Lesson 5: Ethics in managing the project

LESSON 5: ETHICS IN MANAGING THE PROJECT
========================================

## What you will learn
• Explain ethical practices in a school enterprise.
• Show how records protect honesty.

Curriculum outcomes: c) uphold ethics and collective efforts in managing enterprise projects at school

## Introduction
Suppose the class sells vegetables for 300 shillings and the record shows only 200. The missing money is not a small mistake. It is a break of trust.

## Notes
Ethics are rules about what is right and fair. In a school enterprise, ethics protect the learners, the customers and the money.

### Practices to keep
- Honesty: record every item taken from the store and every shilling received or spent. Do not hide sales.
- Accountability: be ready to explain your actions. If you were on the watering team, you should be able to say whether you watered.
- No stealing: project tools, produce and money are not personal property.
- Fair shares: do not give the easy jobs to friends and the hard jobs to everyone else.
- Truthful selling: do not pretend that small seedlings are bigger than they are, or that spoiled vegetables are fresh.
- Care of tools: wash them, return them and report breakages.
- Agreed use of income: money might buy more seed, repair a tool or support a school need the class and teacher agreed. It is not for sweets for one group.
- Respect: speak politely to customers, including younger learners and workers.
- Inclusion: learners with disabilities take roles they can do well. Nobody is left out because of gender.

### A simple record
Date, item, money in, money out, and the balance. If you received 100 shillings and spent 40, the balance is 60 shillings. The teacher checks the record with the treasurer. Two people seeing the same numbers makes cheating harder and mistakes easier to find.

When a mistake happens, correct it in the open. Hiding it makes it worse. Integrity is doing the right thing even when nobody is watching the garden.

## Key words
• ethics — rules about what is right and fair
• accountability — being ready to explain what you did with a duty or with money
• balance — the money left after spending is subtracted from money received

## Worked examples

### Example 1
The class receives 80 shillings and spends 30 shillings on seed. What is the balance?

Working:
1. Subtract spending from money received.
2. 80 minus 30 is 50.

Answer: 50 shillings.

### Example 2
A learner takes two cobs home without recording them. Which ethical rule is broken?

Working:
1. The cobs belong to the project.
2. Nothing was written in the record.

Answer: Honesty. Project produce is not personal property, and every item taken should be recorded.

## Activity: Our ethics charter
You will need: Manila paper, Marker pens, A notebook for records
1. Discuss ethical practices the class will observe while managing the project.
2. Write five rules on a charter and display it near the project.
3. Draw a record table with columns for date, item, money in, money out and balance.
4. Practise one row with the prices from your plan.
5. Agree what the class will do if a rule is broken: tell the teacher and correct the record.

## Practice
1. Give three ethical practices in a school enterprise.
2. Money in is 150 shillings and money out is 45 shillings. What is the balance?
3. What is accountability?

## Summary
• Ethics keep the project fair and trusted.
• Record money in, money out and the balance, and let the teacher check it.
• Correct mistakes in the open.

### Answers to practice
1. Any three: honest records, no stealing, fair duties, truthful selling, agreed use of money, and including everyone.
2. 105 shillings.
3. Being ready to explain what you did with your duty or with project money.

PAGE 7: Lesson 6: Safety items from local materials

LESSON 6: SAFETY ITEMS FROM LOCAL MATERIALS
===========================================

## What you will learn
• Design simple personal protective items for road safety using local materials.
• Explain how the items can be part of a school enterprise or campaign.

Curriculum outcomes: a) identify the projects that can be initiated at school; b) participate in initiating an enterprise project at school

## Introduction
A driver sees a bright colour long before a dark uniform disappears into the evening. A simple sash made at school can help a walking group be seen near a busy road.

## Notes
Personal protective equipment, often called PPE, is clothing or an item that reduces the chance of harm. On the road, the most useful protection for a learner is to be seen early, and to know where to walk.

The class can design these items from materials that are easy to find. This can be the school enterprise itself, or one product of a larger project.

### Items you can design
- A bright sash or armband from coloured cloth or strong paper, worn across the chest so drivers see the group
- A small handheld sign reading 'Children walking', made from cardboard and a stick, for the teacher or an older guide at the front of the line
- Shiny strips cut from clean foil packets or reflective tape, stuck on the sash

Design them. Do not stand in the road to test them, and do not direct traffic. Learners walk on the side of the road with an adult. The sign is for the adult guide, not an invitation for a child to stop vehicles.

### Making the design viable
List materials and cost, just as you did for the garden. If each sash needs a strip of cloth the school already has, the money cost may be zero. Time is still a cost: agree how many sashes to make so that the work fits one or two lessons.

### Using the items well
- Wear them when the class walks together near a road, with a teacher
- Use authorised school transport when the school provides it, rather than stopping unknown vehicles
- Keep the sashes at school so they are not lost
- If you sell a few at a school event, record the money

A good design is bright, strong enough not to tear at once, and comfortable to wear. Test the brightness in the school field, not on the road.

## Key words
• personal protective equipment — clothing or an item worn or carried to reduce harm
• sash — a bright strip of cloth worn across the body so that a person is easy to see
• reflective — able to shine light back so that it is seen in dim conditions

## Worked examples

### Example 1
A group makes dark brown armbands for a walk beside a busy road. Why is the design weak?

Working:
1. Drivers need to see the walkers early.
2. Dark colours blend into the surroundings.

Answer: The armbands are not bright, so drivers may not see the learners in time.

### Example 2
Who should hold a 'Children walking' sign near the road?

Working:
1. Stopping or guiding traffic is an adult's task.
2. Learners stay with the walking group.

Answer: The teacher or another adult guide, not a learner standing in the road.

## Activity: Design a road-safety sash
You will need: Bright cloth or paper, Scissors used with the teacher, Cardboard, Crayons, Glue or tape
1. In groups, design a sash or armband and a model sign using local materials.
2. Choose bright colours and write a short safety message.
3. Make one sample in class. Keep scissors with the teacher.
4. Show the sample in the school field and ask whether it can be seen from a distance.
5. Write the materials and the cost, even if the cost is zero, in the project record.

## Practice
1. What is personal protective equipment for road safety, in this lesson?
2. Why are bright colours better than dark colours for a sash?
3. Where should learners test the sash?

## Summary
• A bright sash helps a walking group to be seen.
• Design and test it in school, and let an adult lead any walk near a road.
• The design can be a small school enterprise if materials and time allow.

### Answers to practice
1. A bright item such as a sash or armband that helps walkers be seen, or a sign carried by an adult guide.
2. Drivers can see bright colours sooner.
3. In the school field or compound, with a teacher, not by standing in the road.

PAGE 8: Lesson 7: Showcasing and judging success

LESSON 7: SHOWCASING AND JUDGING SUCCESS
========================================

## What you will learn
• Showcase the school enterprise to others.
• Evaluate whether the project met its goal and its ethics.

Curriculum outcomes: b) participate in initiating an enterprise project at school; c) uphold ethics and collective efforts in managing enterprise projects at school

## Introduction
At the end of a project, the class has more than plants or sashes. It has a story of what worked, what failed and what should change next time.

## Notes
To showcase a project is to show it to other people so they can see the product and hear how it was managed. A showcase can be a table at assembly, a display in class, or a short talk to another class.

### What to show
- The product: vegetables, seedlings, crafts or safety sashes
- The plan: the goal and the cost
- The record: money in, money out and the balance, checked by the teacher
- The roles: who did what, without boasting or leaving people out
- One problem you solved, and one thing you would do differently

Speak honestly. If some seedlings died, say so, and say what you learned about water or shade. Pretending that everything succeeded breaks the ethics you agreed.

### Evaluating success
Ask these questions together:

- Did we produce what the plan promised?
- Did we stay within the cost?
- Did everyone do a fair share?
- Was the record complete?
- Did we keep people and tools safe?
- Did we care for the soil, water and any animals?
- Should we continue, change, or stop this project next term?

Success is not only profit. A garden that fed the feeding programme and taught the class to keep records has succeeded even if only a little money was left. A project that made money but hid the records has failed the ethics test.

Thank the workers, the teacher and anyone who gave materials. Then store tools properly so the next group can begin without buying everything again.

## Key words
• showcase — to display a project and explain how it was done
• evaluate — to judge how well something succeeded
• profit — money left after the costs have been paid

## Worked examples

### Example 1
The class grew vegetables and kept a full record, but earned only 20 shillings after costs. Have they failed? Explain.

Working:
1. The goal was to grow vegetables and to learn management.
2. The record was honest.
3. Profit was small but the ethics held.

Answer: They have not simply failed. They produced food and kept honest records. Next time they can ask how to improve the harvest.

### Example 2
A showcase speech says every plant grew perfectly, but the secretary's book shows many plants wilted. What should the class do?

Working:
1. The speech and the record disagree.
2. Ethics require the truth.

Answer: Correct the speech so that it matches the record, and explain what they learned.

## Activity: Showcase the project
You will need: The product or photos of it, The plan and the record book, A table or display space
1. Prepare a short talk: goal, what you did, the balance, one problem and one lesson.
2. Display the product and the ethics charter.
3. Showcase the project to another class or at assembly.
4. Invite questions and answer them from the record, not from guesses.
5. As a class, decide whether to continue, change or stop the project, and write the decision.

## Practice
1. What does it mean to showcase a project?
2. Name three questions used to evaluate a school enterprise.
3. Why is a complete money record part of a good showcase?

## Summary
• A showcase shows the product, the plan and the record.
• Evaluate the goal, the cost, fairness, safety and honesty.
• Tell the truth about problems, and decide what to do next term.

### Answers to practice
1. To show the product and explain how the project was planned and managed.
2. Any three: Did we meet the goal? Did we keep to the cost? Were duties fair? Was the record complete? Were people safe? Should we continue?
3. It shows honesty and lets others trust the balance the class reports.

REVISION QUIZ — 4.3 ENTERPRISE PROJECT AT SCHOOL
========================================

Answer all the questions, then mark yourself on the Answers tab.

1. A school enterprise is:
   A. A project learners and teachers run to produce something useful
   B. A county law
   C. A type of wild animal
   D. A school punishment

2. Which project is suitable for a primary school?
   A. A vegetable garden
   B. A stone quarry that replaces lessons
   C. Mining with explosives
   D. Sending learners to work in a factory all week

3. A viable project is one that:
   A. Can succeed with the space, money and time the school has
   B. Needs things the school can never get
   C. Must make a huge profit in one day
   D. Has no plan

4. Seeds cost 35 shillings and a notebook costs 15 shillings. The start-up cost is:
   A. 20 shillings
   B. 50 shillings
   C. 15 shillings
   D. 35 shillings

5. The treasurer should:
   A. Keep project money at home
   B. Record money with the teacher and leave it at school
   C. Hide some sales
   D. Spend the money on sweets for friends

6. Collective effort means:
   A. One person does everything
   B. The class shares the work towards one goal
   C. Nobody has a duty
   D. Only the chairperson may speak

7. Which action follows enterprise ethics?
   A. Recording every sale
   B. Taking produce home in secret
   C. Giving all hard jobs to one group
   D. Changing the balance so the record looks better

8. Money in is 200 shillings and money out is 80 shillings. The balance is:
   A. 280 shillings
   B. 120 shillings
   C. 80 shillings
   D. 200 shillings

9. A road-safety sash should be:
   A. Bright, so that walkers are seen
   B. As dark as possible
   C. Tested by standing in the middle of the road
   D. Used by a learner to stop cars

10. A project with honest records and a small harvest can still be a success because:

11. What should a showcase include?
   A. The product, the plan and the money record
   B. Only a claim that nothing went wrong
   C. The treasurer's pocket
   D. A list of learners who were left out on purpose
pages.answers:
ANSWERS — 4.3 ENTERPRISE PROJECT AT SCHOOL
========================================

1. A. A project learners and teachers run to produce something useful
   The class produces goods or a service and learns how to manage the work.

2. A. A vegetable garden
   A garden can be managed at school with a teacher. Dangerous work that replaces school is not suitable.

3. A. Can succeed with the space, money and time the school has
   Viable means the idea fits what the school can actually do.

4. B. 50 shillings
   35 + 15 = 50 shillings.

5. B. Record money with the teacher and leave it at school
   Project money stays at school and every amount is recorded.

6. B. The class shares the work towards one goal
   Each learner takes a role so the project does not depend on one person.

7. A. Recording every sale
   Honest records are a basic ethical practice.

8. B. 120 shillings
   200 minus 80 is 120 shillings.

9. A. Bright, so that walkers are seen
   Bright colours help drivers see a group. Testing belongs in the school compound, and an adult leads any walk.

10. Success includes learning to manage work fairly and truthfully, not only a large profit.
   The class evaluates the goal, the ethics and the product together.

11. A. The product, the plan and the money record
   Visitors should see what was made and how it was managed.

studyPages.title: Overview
studyPages.body:
OVERVIEW
========

An enterprise is a small project people start in order to produce something useful and, often, to earn some income. In this sub-strand you will identify projects a school can start, help to plan and run one, share the work fairly, and keep honest records.

## Strand 4.0: Resources and Economic Activities
Sub-strand 4.3: Enterprise Project at School
Suggested lessons: 7

## Learning outcomes
By the end of the sub-strand, the learner should be able to:
a) identify the projects that can be initiated at school
b) participate in initiating an enterprise project at school
c) uphold ethics and collective efforts in managing enterprise projects at school

## Key inquiry questions
1. How are enterprise projects managed in school?

## Core competencies
• Communication and collaboration: Learners share responsibilities on the planned enterprise
• Creativity and imagination: Learners identify a viable project enterprise at school

## Values
• Responsibility: Learners engage in the assigned roles and duties as they undertake the enterprise project at school and evaluate its success
• Integrity: Learners develop accountability as they participate in the initiation and management of the enterprise project in the school

## Pertinent and contemporary issues
• Creative and critical thinking: Learners undertake the enterprise project at school and showcase the outcomes.

## Links to other learning areas
• Mathematics: Learners plan and undertake a viable enterprise project at school.

## Source
• KICD Grade 4 Social Studies Curriculum Design (Revised 2024) — Strand 4.0 Resources and Economic Activities, Sub-strand 4.3 Enterprise Project at School

studyPages.title: Lesson 1: Projects a school can start
studyPages.body:
LESSON 1: PROJECTS A SCHOOL CAN START
=====================================

## What you will learn
• Explain what an enterprise project is.
• Identify projects that can be started at school.

Curriculum outcomes: a) identify the projects that can be initiated at school

## Introduction
Some schools grow vegetables behind the classrooms and sell the extra to teachers and parents. The garden is not only a farm. It is a small business that learners help to run.

## Notes
An enterprise is a project started to produce goods or services. A school enterprise is run by learners and teachers together, on the school grounds or with the school's permission. The aim is to learn how work is planned, to produce something useful, and sometimes to raise a little money for the project or the school.

### Projects that suit a primary school
A project should be possible for learners of your age, with adults nearby:

- A vegetable garden, selling surplus sukuma wiki, tomatoes or onions
- A tree nursery, raising seedlings to plant or sell
- Poultry, such as a few chickens, if the school has a safe house for them and an adult in charge
- Crafts, such as woven mats, decorated cards or simple beadwork using local materials
- A recycling project that collects clean bottles or paper for sale to a buyer
- Making simple road-safety items, such as bright sashes, to use in a school safety campaign or to sell at a school event

Not every idea is suitable. A project that needs dangerous machines, takes learners out of class for whole days, or breaks the law is not a school enterprise.

### How to spot a possible project
Look at what the school already has: land, water, learners who can work, and people who might buy the product. Also look at a need. If the road near school is busy, a safety campaign may be useful. If the kitchen buys vegetables every week, a garden may have a ready market.

## Key words
• enterprise — a project started to produce goods or services, often to earn some income
• project — a planned piece of work with a goal
• surplus — what is left after the producers have taken what they need

## Worked examples

### Example 1
Learners want to open a stone quarry and miss lessons to break rocks. Is this a suitable school enterprise?

Working:
1. The work is dangerous.
2. It takes children out of school.
3. Forcing children to do such work is child labour.

Answer: No. It is dangerous, it replaces learning, and it is not lawful child work.

### Example 2
The school kitchen buys vegetables every week, and there is an empty plot with water nearby. Suggest one enterprise.

Working:
1. There is land, water and a buyer.

Answer: A vegetable garden.

## Activity: Brainstorm school enterprises
You will need: Manila paper, Marker pens
1. In groups, brainstorm enterprise projects that can be undertaken at your school.
2. For each idea, write what you would produce and who might use or buy it.
3. Cross out any idea that is dangerous or would stop you attending lessons.
4. Present three possible projects to the class.

## Practice
1. What is a school enterprise project?
2. Name three projects a school could start.
3. Why is a quarry project not suitable for Grade 4 learners?

## Summary
• A school enterprise produces something useful and teaches learners how work is organised.
• Gardens, nurseries, crafts and recycling can fit a primary school.
• Dangerous work that replaces lessons is not a school project.

### Answers to practice
1. A project run by learners and teachers to produce goods or services and to learn how a small business is managed.
2. Any three: a vegetable garden, a tree nursery, poultry, crafts, recycling, or making simple road-safety items.
3. It is dangerous and it would take children away from school.

studyPages.title: Lesson 2: Choosing a viable project
studyPages.body:
LESSON 2: CHOOSING A VIABLE PROJECT
===================================

## What you will learn
• Explain what makes a project viable.
• Choose one viable enterprise for the class or school.

Curriculum outcomes: a) identify the projects that can be initiated at school; b) participate in initiating an enterprise project at school

## Introduction
A good idea can still fail if there is no water, no buyer or no one to do the work. Viable means the project can actually succeed with what you have.

## Notes
A viable project is one that can work. Before the class begins, test the idea with simple questions.

### Questions that test an idea
- Need: do people want this product or service?
- Resources: do we have land, water, materials or a safe space?
- Skills: can learners do the work with a teacher helping?
- Time: can the work be done at agreed times without missing lessons?
- Cost: can the school or parents provide the first materials, or can we start very small?
- Market: who will use or buy the product?
- Rules: has the head teacher agreed? Does the project obey the law and school rules?
- Care: will the project harm the soil, waste water or leave animals without shelter? If yes, change the plan.

### Comparing ideas
Write two or three ideas in a table. Give each question a yes or a no. The idea with more yes answers is the stronger one. If a garden has land and a buyer but a poultry house would cost more than the school can raise, the garden is more viable this term.

Creativity is useful here. A class with no spare land might grow vegetables in sacks, or make cards from used paper. A small start is wiser than a huge plan that stops in the first week.

The class should agree together. Forcing one group’s idea on everyone, without listening, makes the project hard to manage later.

## Key words
• viable — able to succeed with the resources and time available
• market — the people who will use or buy what you produce
• cost — the money or materials needed to start and run a project

## Worked examples

### Example 1
Idea A needs a borehole the school does not have. Idea B uses rainwater already stored in a tank. Which is more viable this term, and why?

Working:
1. Idea A depends on something the school cannot provide now.
2. Idea B uses water the school already has.

Answer: Idea B, because the water it needs is already available.

### Example 2
A class wants to keep ten cows. They have a small flower bed and no grazing. What should they decide?

Working:
1. Cows need space and feed the school does not have.

Answer: The project is not viable. They should choose a smaller project, such as vegetables in sacks or a tree nursery.

## Activity: Choose one viable enterprise
You will need: Manila paper, The list of ideas from the previous lesson
1. Draw a table with your best three ideas.
2. Answer yes or no for need, resources, skills, time, cost, market and the head teacher's permission.
3. Choose the idea with the most yes answers.
4. Tell the class why it is viable and what you will produce.

## Practice
1. What does viable mean?
2. Name four things to check before starting a school enterprise.
3. Why might sack gardens be a better start than a large farm?

## Summary
• A viable project fits the school's space, money, time and skills.
• Compare ideas before choosing.
• Start small enough to finish.

### Answers to practice
1. Able to succeed with the time, skills and resources the school actually has.
2. Any four: need, resources, skills, time, cost, buyers, permission and care for the environment.
3. They need little space and little money, so the class can manage them.

studyPages.title: Lesson 3: Planning the enterprise
studyPages.body:
LESSON 3: PLANNING THE ENTERPRISE
=================================

## What you will learn
• List the materials, costs and steps of a school enterprise.
• Use simple addition to find the cost of the plan.

Curriculum outcomes: b) participate in initiating an enterprise project at school

## Introduction
A garden does not appear because the class likes vegetables. Someone must list the seeds, the tools, the watering days and what to do if the rain fails.

## Notes
A plan is a list of steps written before the work begins. It stops the class from forgetting tools, overspending or arguing about who should do what.

### What the plan contains
- The goal: what we will produce, and by when
- Materials: seeds, tins, soil, water, paper, cloth or feed
- Where the materials will come from: school store, home, or a small purchase
- Cost: the price of anything that must be bought
- A calendar: which days the class will work, and for how long
- Roles: who leads, who records, who handles any money, who does each task
- Permission: the head teacher's signature or spoken agreement
- A rule for profit: if anything is sold, where the money will go

### Counting the cost
Add the prices of the items you must buy. If seeds cost 50 shillings and a watering can costs 200 shillings, the start-up cost is 250 shillings. Items brought from home have a cost of zero shillings in the school record, but you still list them so that nobody forgets.

If the total is more than the class can raise, reduce the plan. Ten packets of seed may be too many. Two packets may be enough for a first bed.

Write the plan neatly. Mathematics helps here: adding costs, counting seedlings and sharing tasks in equal turns. A plan that lives only in somebody's head is easily forgotten or changed unfairly.

## Key words
• plan — steps written down before work begins
• start-up cost — the money needed to begin a project
• goal — what the project is trying to achieve

## Worked examples

### Example 1
Seeds cost 40 shillings, string costs 20 shillings and a notebook for records costs 30 shillings. What is the start-up cost?

Working:
1. Add the three prices.
2. 40 + 20 = 60, and 60 + 30 = 90.

Answer: 90 shillings.

### Example 2
The class needs 500 shillings but can only raise 200. What should they do?

Working:
1. The plan costs more than they have.
2. A smaller plan may still be viable.

Answer: Reduce the plan so that the cost is not more than 200 shillings.

## Activity: Write the project plan
You will need: Exercise book, Prices from a local shop or from the teacher, Manila paper
1. Write the goal of the viable project you chose.
2. List materials. Mark which ones you already have and which must be bought.
3. Add the costs of the items to be bought.
4. Write the steps from the first day to the day you will showcase the product.
5. Show the plan to the teacher and correct anything that is missing.

## Practice
1. Name four things a project plan should contain.
2. Tins cost 15 shillings and seeds cost 25 shillings. What is the total?
3. Why should the plan be written down?

## Summary
• A plan lists the goal, materials, cost, time and roles.
• Add costs before you begin, and shrink the plan if it is too expensive.
• The head teacher should agree to the plan.

### Answers to practice
1. Any four: the goal, materials, costs, calendar, roles, permission and a rule for any money earned.
2. 40 shillings.
3. So that steps, costs and duties are not forgotten or changed unfairly.

studyPages.title: Lesson 4: Sharing the work
studyPages.body:
LESSON 4: SHARING THE WORK
==========================

## What you will learn
• Share responsibilities for the enterprise.
• Explain why collective effort helps a project succeed.

Curriculum outcomes: b) participate in initiating an enterprise project at school; c) uphold ethics and collective efforts in managing enterprise projects at school

## Introduction
If only one learner waters the garden, the work stops whenever that learner is absent. When the class shares the duties, the project can continue.

## Notes
Collective effort means working together towards one goal. Each person does a part, and the parts add up to the finished project.

### Useful roles
Schools may use these roles. The names can change, but the duties should be clear:

- Chairperson: calls the group to order and makes sure everyone is heard
- Secretary: writes decisions, dates and work done
- Treasurer: keeps the money record with the teacher. Learners do not take project money home.
- Team leaders: each watches one task, such as watering, weeding, collecting materials or preparing the showcase

Roles should rotate so that many learners learn each skill. A role is a duty, not a chance to boss others or to escape work.

### Starting the work
On the first day, gather the materials in the plan, mark the plot or the workspace, and do the first task together. The teacher stays with the class. At the end, the secretary records what was done and what is needed next time.

### When someone is away
Agree a substitute before you need one. If the watering team is at a match, another team waters. Collective effort fails when people say 'that is not my work' while the plants dry up.

Listen to quiet learners as well as to loud ones. A good idea about pests or about a cheaper material can come from anybody.

## Key words
• collective effort — people working together, each doing a share of the task
• role — the duty a person is given in a group
• treasurer — the person who keeps the record of money, together with the teacher

## Worked examples

### Example 1
The treasurer wants to keep the project money in a pocket over the weekend. What should happen instead?

Working:
1. Project money can be lost or misused.
2. The teacher is responsible with the learners.

Answer: The money should stay in the school office or with the teacher, and the record should be written the same day.

### Example 2
Only the chairperson has been allowed to speak for three weeks. What is wrong?

Working:
1. Collective effort needs many voices.
2. Roles should not silence the group.

Answer: Other learners are not being heard. The chairperson should invite them to speak, and roles should be shared.

## Activity: Share responsibilities
You will need: The project plan, Exercise book
1. List the tasks in the plan.
2. Agree roles: chairperson, secretary, treasurer with the teacher, and task teams.
3. Write each person's duty for the next two weeks.
4. Decide who covers a task if someone is absent.
5. Start the first task together and let the secretary record it.

## Practice
1. What is collective effort?
2. What does the secretary do?
3. Why should project money stay at school?

## Summary
• Shared roles keep the project going when one person is away.
• The treasurer works with the teacher and does not take money home.
• Everyone should be heard.

### Answers to practice
1. Working together so that each person does a share of the project.
2. Writes down decisions, dates and the work that has been done.
3. So that it is not lost or used for a private purpose, and so that the record stays with the project.

studyPages.title: Lesson 5: Ethics in managing the project
studyPages.body:
LESSON 5: ETHICS IN MANAGING THE PROJECT
========================================

## What you will learn
• Explain ethical practices in a school enterprise.
• Show how records protect honesty.

Curriculum outcomes: c) uphold ethics and collective efforts in managing enterprise projects at school

## Introduction
Suppose the class sells vegetables for 300 shillings and the record shows only 200. The missing money is not a small mistake. It is a break of trust.

## Notes
Ethics are rules about what is right and fair. In a school enterprise, ethics protect the learners, the customers and the money.

### Practices to keep
- Honesty: record every item taken from the store and every shilling received or spent. Do not hide sales.
- Accountability: be ready to explain your actions. If you were on the watering team, you should be able to say whether you watered.
- No stealing: project tools, produce and money are not personal property.
- Fair shares: do not give the easy jobs to friends and the hard jobs to everyone else.
- Truthful selling: do not pretend that small seedlings are bigger than they are, or that spoiled vegetables are fresh.
- Care of tools: wash them, return them and report breakages.
- Agreed use of income: money might buy more seed, repair a tool or support a school need the class and teacher agreed. It is not for sweets for one group.
- Respect: speak politely to customers, including younger learners and workers.
- Inclusion: learners with disabilities take roles they can do well. Nobody is left out because of gender.

### A simple record
Date, item, money in, money out, and the balance. If you received 100 shillings and spent 40, the balance is 60 shillings. The teacher checks the record with the treasurer. Two people seeing the same numbers makes cheating harder and mistakes easier to find.

When a mistake happens, correct it in the open. Hiding it makes it worse. Integrity is doing the right thing even when nobody is watching the garden.

## Key words
• ethics — rules about what is right and fair
• accountability — being ready to explain what you did with a duty or with money
• balance — the money left after spending is subtracted from money received

## Worked examples

### Example 1
The class receives 80 shillings and spends 30 shillings on seed. What is the balance?

Working:
1. Subtract spending from money received.
2. 80 minus 30 is 50.

Answer: 50 shillings.

### Example 2
A learner takes two cobs home without recording them. Which ethical rule is broken?

Working:
1. The cobs belong to the project.
2. Nothing was written in the record.

Answer: Honesty. Project produce is not personal property, and every item taken should be recorded.

## Activity: Our ethics charter
You will need: Manila paper, Marker pens, A notebook for records
1. Discuss ethical practices the class will observe while managing the project.
2. Write five rules on a charter and display it near the project.
3. Draw a record table with columns for date, item, money in, money out and balance.
4. Practise one row with the prices from your plan.
5. Agree what the class will do if a rule is broken: tell the teacher and correct the record.

## Practice
1. Give three ethical practices in a school enterprise.
2. Money in is 150 shillings and money out is 45 shillings. What is the balance?
3. What is accountability?

## Summary
• Ethics keep the project fair and trusted.
• Record money in, money out and the balance, and let the teacher check it.
• Correct mistakes in the open.

### Answers to practice
1. Any three: honest records, no stealing, fair duties, truthful selling, agreed use of money, and including everyone.
2. 105 shillings.
3. Being ready to explain what you did with your duty or with project money.

studyPages.title: Lesson 6: Safety items from local materials
studyPages.body:
LESSON 6: SAFETY ITEMS FROM LOCAL MATERIALS
===========================================

## What you will learn
• Design simple personal protective items for road safety using local materials.
• Explain how the items can be part of a school enterprise or campaign.

Curriculum outcomes: a) identify the projects that can be initiated at school; b) participate in initiating an enterprise project at school

## Introduction
A driver sees a bright colour long before a dark uniform disappears into the evening. A simple sash made at school can help a walking group be seen near a busy road.

## Notes
Personal protective equipment, often called PPE, is clothing or an item that reduces the chance of harm. On the road, the most useful protection for a learner is to be seen early, and to know where to walk.

The class can design these items from materials that are easy to find. This can be the school enterprise itself, or one product of a larger project.

### Items you can design
- A bright sash or armband from coloured cloth or strong paper, worn across the chest so drivers see the group
- A small handheld sign reading 'Children walking', made from cardboard and a stick, for the teacher or an older guide at the front of the line
- Shiny strips cut from clean foil packets or reflective tape, stuck on the sash

Design them. Do not stand in the road to test them, and do not direct traffic. Learners walk on the side of the road with an adult. The sign is for the adult guide, not an invitation for a child to stop vehicles.

### Making the design viable
List materials and cost, just as you did for the garden. If each sash needs a strip of cloth the school already has, the money cost may be zero. Time is still a cost: agree how many sashes to make so that the work fits one or two lessons.

### Using the items well
- Wear them when the class walks together near a road, with a teacher
- Use authorised school transport when the school provides it, rather than stopping unknown vehicles
- Keep the sashes at school so they are not lost
- If you sell a few at a school event, record the money

A good design is bright, strong enough not to tear at once, and comfortable to wear. Test the brightness in the school field, not on the road.

## Key words
• personal protective equipment — clothing or an item worn or carried to reduce harm
• sash — a bright strip of cloth worn across the body so that a person is easy to see
• reflective — able to shine light back so that it is seen in dim conditions

## Worked examples

### Example 1
A group makes dark brown armbands for a walk beside a busy road. Why is the design weak?

Working:
1. Drivers need to see the walkers early.
2. Dark colours blend into the surroundings.

Answer: The armbands are not bright, so drivers may not see the learners in time.

### Example 2
Who should hold a 'Children walking' sign near the road?

Working:
1. Stopping or guiding traffic is an adult's task.
2. Learners stay with the walking group.

Answer: The teacher or another adult guide, not a learner standing in the road.

## Activity: Design a road-safety sash
You will need: Bright cloth or paper, Scissors used with the teacher, Cardboard, Crayons, Glue or tape
1. In groups, design a sash or armband and a model sign using local materials.
2. Choose bright colours and write a short safety message.
3. Make one sample in class. Keep scissors with the teacher.
4. Show the sample in the school field and ask whether it can be seen from a distance.
5. Write the materials and the cost, even if the cost is zero, in the project record.

## Practice
1. What is personal protective equipment for road safety, in this lesson?
2. Why are bright colours better than dark colours for a sash?
3. Where should learners test the sash?

## Summary
• A bright sash helps a walking group to be seen.
• Design and test it in school, and let an adult lead any walk near a road.
• The design can be a small school enterprise if materials and time allow.

### Answers to practice
1. A bright item such as a sash or armband that helps walkers be seen, or a sign carried by an adult guide.
2. Drivers can see bright colours sooner.
3. In the school field or compound, with a teacher, not by standing in the road.

studyPages.title: Lesson 7: Showcasing and judging success
studyPages.body:
LESSON 7: SHOWCASING AND JUDGING SUCCESS
========================================

## What you will learn
• Showcase the school enterprise to others.
• Evaluate whether the project met its goal and its ethics.

Curriculum outcomes: b) participate in initiating an enterprise project at school; c) uphold ethics and collective efforts in managing enterprise projects at school

## Introduction
At the end of a project, the class has more than plants or sashes. It has a story of what worked, what failed and what should change next time.

## Notes
To showcase a project is to show it to other people so they can see the product and hear how it was managed. A showcase can be a table at assembly, a display in class, or a short talk to another class.

### What to show
- The product: vegetables, seedlings, crafts or safety sashes
- The plan: the goal and the cost
- The record: money in, money out and the balance, checked by the teacher
- The roles: who did what, without boasting or leaving people out
- One problem you solved, and one thing you would do differently

Speak honestly. If some seedlings died, say so, and say what you learned about water or shade. Pretending that everything succeeded breaks the ethics you agreed.

### Evaluating success
Ask these questions together:

- Did we produce what the plan promised?
- Did we stay within the cost?
- Did everyone do a fair share?
- Was the record complete?
- Did we keep people and tools safe?
- Did we care for the soil, water and any animals?
- Should we continue, change, or stop this project next term?

Success is not only profit. A garden that fed the feeding programme and taught the class to keep records has succeeded even if only a little money was left. A project that made money but hid the records has failed the ethics test.

Thank the workers, the teacher and anyone who gave materials. Then store tools properly so the next group can begin without buying everything again.

## Key words
• showcase — to display a project and explain how it was done
• evaluate — to judge how well something succeeded
• profit — money left after the costs have been paid

## Worked examples

### Example 1
The class grew vegetables and kept a full record, but earned only 20 shillings after costs. Have they failed? Explain.

Working:
1. The goal was to grow vegetables and to learn management.
2. The record was honest.
3. Profit was small but the ethics held.

Answer: They have not simply failed. They produced food and kept honest records. Next time they can ask how to improve the harvest.

### Example 2
A showcase speech says every plant grew perfectly, but the secretary's book shows many plants wilted. What should the class do?

Working:
1. The speech and the record disagree.
2. Ethics require the truth.

Answer: Correct the speech so that it matches the record, and explain what they learned.

## Activity: Showcase the project
You will need: The product or photos of it, The plan and the record book, A table or display space
1. Prepare a short talk: goal, what you did, the balance, one problem and one lesson.
2. Display the product and the ethics charter.
3. Showcase the project to another class or at assembly.
4. Invite questions and answer them from the record, not from guesses.
5. As a class, decide whether to continue, change or stop the project, and write the decision.

## Practice
1. What does it mean to showcase a project?
2. Name three questions used to evaluate a school enterprise.
3. Why is a complete money record part of a good showcase?

## Summary
• A showcase shows the product, the plan and the record.
• Evaluate the goal, the cost, fairness, safety and honesty.
• Tell the truth about problems, and decide what to do next term.

### Answers to practice
1. To show the product and explain how the project was planned and managed.
2. Any three: Did we meet the goal? Did we keep to the cost? Were duties fair? Was the record complete? Were people safe? Should we continue?
3. It shows honesty and lets others trust the balance the class reports.

Sending learners to work in a factory all week

Needs things the school can never get
Must make a huge profit in one day

Spend the money on sweets for friends

questions.explanation: Each learner takes a role so the project does not depend on one person.

Changing the balance so the record looks better
questions.explanation: Honest records are a basic ethical practice.
